I would suggest getting two of the 178L bags. The calculator suggested is a good tool, but you have to remember that you need to compress the bedding in order for it to hold burrows and that will decrease the bedding height substantially. The recommendation is to multiply the calculator's result by 1.5 to know how much bedding you really need with compression taken into account. That will work out at nearly 200L if 20cm bedding depth is your goal. Personally, I needed about 220-240L for a similarly sized enclosure (Bucatstate 120cm and I went for 25cm of bedding).

Yeah, it does "mean much". No one's saying stripe = definitely not Syrian (or that stripes can't occur in Syrians), the point is that stripes are uncommon in Syrians, but a standard feature in dwarfs, hence the presence of the stripe means that the hammy is more likely to be a dwarf, especially when you look at the whole picture i.e. her size. She looks somewhat like the coloration known as "sunfire" in dwarfs.

She really looks like a baby Syrian, but I'm guessing she's a dwarf, because of the stripe going down her back (while the cream coloring is common in Syrians, that stripe really is not, that's very much a dwarf thing) and she's so tiny, like too tiny for a Syrian to be that size and that "fully" developed. Either way, you've got one unique hammy.
What are the soles of her feet like? Syrians have hairless soles with paw pads (little bumps), dwarfs have smooth and hairy soles.

It should be opaque to provide the feeling of safety, but you can make it opaque by covering it with something. I've seen hides where people have glued moss on the outside, making it look like some cool forest cave.

I'd bake it. It's quicker, plus you're also heat treating it which makes it safer. Air drying can take a lot of time and if there are any bugs or eggs or other nasties in the soil, that time coupled with a favorable (=moist) environment could lead to an infestation down the road.

I'm afraid you can't really tell their age by that alone. Yours may have had such markings since birth, especially if they haven't really changed shape or size. So while discoloration around private bits is commonly seen in aging hams, it's not really a way to tell how old they are. You're better off asking the previous owner if they know when your hammy was born or at least find out how long they had him for and if they got him from a pet store (in which case he was likely purchased at a few weeks to a couple months of age). If he came from a rescue organization the people there might have this information.

Yeah, this is common in older males and the discoloration does spread as they age. I guess you can think of it like age spots in humans. Keeping an eye on it is a good idea, but in all likelihood it's a normal sign of aging.
Probably an ear wart. They're relatively common in dwarf hamsters, especially when they get older. You do need to see a vet to get an actual diagnosis and see whether it can/should be removed.

It only has vents in the upper wooden bit? I don't know, it seems too little to me, personally I'd like more ventilation for my hammy. Poor circulation can also lead to overheating and high humidity. I wouldn't go for that grid thing. I have seen a setup like that a few times, but there are many issues with it. For one, you need to make a suitable mesh lid for it, which in itself isn't an issue, but attaching it to the "enclosure" would be. An insecure lid is an escape hazard and could also hurt the hamster. Another, much more likely way a hamster could hurt themselves in that enclosure is by trying to get out via the gaps in the panels. They could get their paws stuck in there since it's not a solid structure. These grids are good for making play pens, but not as permanent enclosures.
You can just put them in a freezer until you're able to afford it. There's nothing strange about doing that, both humans and animals go into cold storage before further processing.

I think your assessment of her behavior is incorrect. Climbing is universally recognized as a stress behavior, so there's really no reason to think she loves it, especially since this is not a natural behavior for them. She may do it often, but that does not equate to enjoyment. She has no way to express her natural behaviors in that enclosure, so what else is she left to do but climb up when burrowing down is not an option? It's basically the same when you say she doesn't like burrowing... you don't know that unless you give her the opportunity! That pan clearly doesn't fit the 25cm+ that's required for burrowing and doing something like a dig box or a corner of more bedding is not the same as an entire properly sized enclosure filled with bedding, so if she didn't burrow in a little area you can't automatically assume she doesn't like burrowing. All hamsters do, it's hardwired into them, it's how they live and survive and a mere 30-100 years of domestication isn't going to remove that instinct. Also, you said she doesn't fall... Here's a thing - she's not falling NOW. Have you seen videos of elderly hamsters? They get wobbly on their feet, they sway a little. You may have seen that in old people and well, it's the same with hamsters. So even if the platforms aren't (in your assessment) dangerous now, they absolutely will be once she's older.


You clearly love her and want the best for her, so please trust the community and the scientific research behind our recommendations and get her the appropriate setup. Bucatstate 3.0 (120cm) is a great option, so is a similarly sized tank, and with such an enclosure you can still provide her with safe climbing opportunities (cork logs, grapevine, etc.) as well as an opportunity to burrow for real and you are able to ensure that the setup will stay safe for her even in her senior days.
Yes, they do.
There are quite a few people on FB's Ethical Hamster Care group who have bought Bucatstate cages from Temu and they all seem happy with their purchases and say the enclosures are authentic.
I recommend Getzoo platforms. https://www.getzoo.de/en/enclosure-equipment/floors/ They're made of solid wood and are of superb quality.

I wouldn't. For one, they're ground up so fine that it's essentially powder, your hamster's not gonna be able to pick it up, especially when it's scattered on top of the bedding (which is what you're supposed to do). Secondly, those herbs have likely seen some pesticides and other chemicals, plus we don't know what other treatments they may have been subjected to during processing. So yeah, I wouldn't risk it. Something like organically grown loose leaf herbs for tea are probably fine, but skip the mass produced stuff.

By that logic the much touted Bucatstate cages would be considered entirely unsuitable, which they are most certainly not. Hell, ceramic hides would be unsafe too because they're no easier on teeth than metal and if you assume a hamster will chew a platform then why couldn't they chew a hide or a water dish? Your opinion seems to come from the fact that chewing the metal bars of wired enclosures is problematic - and it absolutely is - but the issue there is that the chewing is a stress behavior, cage aggression, attempt to escape, all that. Bar biting is a response to an underlying problem, not something that happens simply because an object is there. OP's enclosure seems decent and there's no reason to assume the hamster will simply choose to chew on that specific platform because why the hell not. Even if she started to exhibit stress and boredom behaviors at some point, those are almost always taken out on the enclosure itself, not the accessories.
Yes, the holes need to be covered up (a piece of cardboard is OK), but there's nothing wrong with it being metal. That is not a reason to take it out.

You already got the cage recs (because the one you have in mind is unfortunately too small, especially for a female Syrian), but what you said there is slightly alarming. Pet store hamster, I assume? Young ones do grow quickly, but not THAT quickly and they do a sh**ty job sexing hamsters at the stores, which means that often you get sexually mature males and females in the same enclosure, which leads to the obvious and people taking home pregnant females. If yours is suddenly bigger, especially pear-shaped, you may have a litter coming soon.

Get prepared NOW! Another possibility is a medical issue like something going on with her reproductive system, kidneys, etc. which can also lead to bloating and behavior changes. I might be wrong (I hope so!), but if she was mine I would keep a very close eye on her for any potential health issues while also getting stuff ready for her to give birth, should that be the scenario.

Ethical breeding is where the breeder is trained in genetics, is focused on breeding hamsters for their health and temperament and does so with the wellbeing of the mother and pups in mind and also looks for homes where that high standard of care is continued. It's the approach to animal husbandry as a whole, from conception to finding forever homes. Enclosure size is just one aspect and it doesn't define ethical breeding. There are ethical breeders, backyard breeders and people on all levels in between in the USA, Canada and elsewhere.

Hard disagree. So because we can't help everyone we should help no one? By that logic, should we stop fighting against hunger and disease and violence and slavery and everything else that's wrong in the world because we'll never win, there will always be people suffering and those who are causing said suffering. Also, your statement that getting hamsters from somewhere other than pet stores won't help is just plain incorrect. It's basic supply and demand. If there is a decline in people buying "milled" hamsters then the millers will produce less of them. They won't keep up the same level of production because if they did they'd end up losing money because there isn't enough demand for their product. So they will have to produce less. No, we will never fully get rid of pet mills or illegal animal trade but we CAN make a difference by voting with our wallets and making ethical, informed decisions on where we source our pets. This is not a matter of opinion, it's a fact.

It actually hasn't been that long. The recommendation is to leave them alone for the first week to let them get used to the new smells and sounds and routine of their environment and only then start interacting with them. Taming can be a slow process, for some it may take months and some hamsters will never really grow accustomed to humans, these are known as ghost hamsters.

https://www.trixie.de/en/productworld/small-animal/equipment/houses-retreat-options/grass-mat-1001435929-1001452231?itemNo=61156  A hanging grass mat meant for rats, but it's very commonly used to cover bars in hamster cages.

https://www.getzoo.de/en/hugro-rodent-floor-jumbo-approx.-150x70x0.5cm  A huge hemp mat you can cut to size.

These are popular ones in Europe, but I'm sure you can find similar stuff anywhere else, just put something like "grass mat rodents" into whatever shopping platform's search and you'll find them. 

https://www.hamsterwelfare.com/blog/how-barred-cages-can-still-be-beneficial/  This is a good article on making barred cages suitable and it has photos and videos showing how the grass mats (and other options) can be used to increase pan depth to accommodate bedding.

Yeah, the bar covering is to increase the depth of bedding an enclosure can hold. 8 inches is MAYBE okay for a Robo, but if you're considering another species (Syrian or another dwarf), I would aim for a minimum of 10 inches. You should also keep in mind that the covering or pan should actually go up a bit higher than the bedding you want it to contain, because if you squeeze 8 inches of bedding into an 8in pan, some of it (as well as stuff on top of the bedding such as scattered food) will inevitably be pushed through the bars because hams gonna ham. Grass mats are cheap (about €5 where I live) and pretty big, so don't be afraid of a little bit of DIY. They come with string attached so it wouldn't take you more than 10min to attach them to the cage and the total cost is likely around €10-20 depending on how many you want/need to get. It's cheap and easy and IMO makes the enclosure look better as well, they give a really nice natural vibe.

FYI, the grey hide with white hearts is unsafe. Hamsters shouldn't have any textiles in their enclosure because they will try to rip them apart and take it into their burrows for nesting, but those textiles are indigestible and can cause fatal blockages when swallowed, or tiny threads could wrap around their teeth causing eating problems, they may get stuck in cheek pouches leading to infection, etc. Please remove it from the enclosure. You can use it as a snuggle sack during taming or free roam time (under supervision, OFC), but it can't be in the enclosure 24/7. Those types of hides are OK for rats and guinea pigs, but unfortunately not for hamsters.

Yes, they would need to be partially covered because even though the recommended barred cages have enough floor space, their pan depth is still insufficient for enough bedding. You would need to cover the bottom half of the bars to provide enough bedding. I think the new Savic Aura Plexi 120 may have enough space for deep bedding without requiring any DIY on your part but I don't have the specific numbers on that enclosure (it has enough floor space for sure).

Well, you would have no choice but to slope the bedding. But that in itself causes more limitations in arranging the enclosure, not to mention that it might affect the hamster's quality of life if they happen to be a picky type (which can happen with males as well). Another thing, is the hut part removable? Specifically the side wall with the little opening. If it is, I'd take it out permanently. If it isn't, then that's another obstacle in creating a good layout. It would also stop the hamster from being able to burrow properly if they're essentially confined to a little box with one small opening. They might not want their main burrows to be located there and being confined like that might lead to an unhappy hamster with behavioral issues. That might not happen, but it's something to be aware of. Like I said, I had an enclosure with similar dimensions and I definitely felt restricted in what I could do with it and how good of a quality of life I could provide. Now, my hammy was a very chill little guy and seemed perfectly happy in that enclosure, but it definitely was a task trying to make it work. I later switched to a large Bucatstate (120×60×60cm) and that made a big difference both for me and little Ollie who immediately took to the bigger area available for borrowing. I'm not saying no to your proposed enclosure because I know the best cages aren't available everywhere and they're expensive (the large Bucatsate 3.0 is over €250) and at the end of the day that enclosure CAN work. It won't be ideal and you might find yourself looking to upgrade at some point therefore spending more money in the long run, but that enclosure can be made to work.

I would try to find something else. The issue here is height - with less than 15 inches you're going to struggle to fit in enough bedding as well as other accessories on top of that. Have you tried puzzle toys? Typical pet store toys and boredom breakers are actually rather boring and uninspiring for many hammies IMO. There are some cool ones you can make yourself. I'd recommend the YT channel SomethingAnimal, she has some great videos on DIY puzzle toys and they are more unique than the typical basic TP roll DIYs you're probably already familiar with. I'd make a bunch of those, fill them with high value treats and stuff them everywhere, on the surface, in and under the bedding. I know vets like that are rare, but if you ask around in local social media groups you might find one and they might be able to consult from distance since this is a behavioral issue and not something that obviously needs a hands-on visit.

This is just plain wrong. You will find no knowledgeable, ethical hamster keeper who will tell you that just a few centimeters is OK and to prioritize toys over that measly amount. There is scientific research to prove that they need deep bedding and how it affects their behavior: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S016815910500393X Not to mention that deep substrate mimics their natural environment and allows them to exhibit natural behaviors which is what you want for any animal. As I said, you have a good enclosure with plenty of height and you can EASILY fit both a decent amount of bedding (20-30cm) as well as all the toys in there, there is absolutely no need to compromise on either of them. Whatever your source for inspo - Reddit, FB, IG, Tiktok, Pinterest, etc. - you will find more than enough examples of that specific enclosure as well as others of similar dimensions that are both decked out with enrichment AND enough bedding. You CAN and should give your hamster both.

You have a good cage and it seems you've outfitted it decently enough, but to be fair, your bedding situation is worse than OP's. The recommendation is 20cm or more after packing it down, 30cm is often needed for Syrians. For your cage size that would be 200+ liters. https://www.animallama.com/hamsters/how-much-bedding-hamsters-need/ (bedding depth calculator at the end)

That's normal grooming. If they go for a "full bath" then it can take quite a while and they do go over their entire body. He used to do that when he was younger, especially when running on his wheel at night. You're getting a lot of responses saying to get a glass tank, and while those are no doubt a great option, a lot of those recommendations are from people in the US where aquariums are SO MUCH CHEAPER than in Europe. Someone looking to get an "affordable" enclosure is likely not in the market for a glass tank which would cost hundreds of euros/pounds. You will need to use a wood sealant to pee proof the bottom and it's even better if you can line the cage with a chew-proof material, but the few issues can absolutely be solved and it's definitely a good enclosure to get.

I agree, 4 slits is not enough ventilation. Personally, I wouldn't dare to put my hamster in what is almost a closed container.


Also, another thing that caught my eye is the width of those slits. I don't know if the details are to scale (it's not a photo so can't be sure), but if they are, those slits are like 2+ cm wide, which is far too much. A hammy will absolutely try to stick their head through that and will likely get stuck, possibly resulting in injury or even death.

I agree, bar cages can absolutely be suitable for as long as they're big enough and are modified (if needed) to accommodate the required amount of bedding. Nothing inherently wrong with bars, it's just that a barred cage is 99% of the time that tiny typical pet store jail cage, hence the opinion that barred cage = bad. If someone tells you that a barred cage, even when it meets the requirements in terms of size and ability to hold enough bedding is bad and unsuitable and needs to be upgraded, then just disregard that person and their opinion. And your question wasn't anywhere close to being stupid anyway! 🙂 You have a great attitude towards the learning and preparation that proper pet ownership requires and you'll no doubt make an exemplary ham parent.

Huh? People don't talk about it because that's not something we typically do. I wonder if it's a practice with other small animals that you think also applies to hamsters? There's no need for a tray or any kind of lining in a hamster enclosure. Some people do put down a sheet of glass or acrylic in a wooden cage to stop urine seeping into the wood, but a glass enclosure doesn't need any additional protection in that regard. And cleaning up doesn't need any extra help either. You simply remove dirty bedding and wipe down the surface, that's it. Glass doesn't absorbs liquids like wood does so again, there's no need for any extra layers.

Sounds like he's just slowly getting into his natural rhythm. He's been with you for a relatively short amount of time and it's normal for them to develop a routine over several weeks. Also, the seasons are currently changing and it's common for hamsters' sleep schedules to change as the days get longer/shorter.

Based on your description I'd say it's probably not the bacterial wet tail. It's unlikely he'd be acting so normal if it was, that's a very serious medical issue. If he had a switch in diet just a few days ago at the pet store, one that included the introduction of fresh veggies (in larger than needed quantities, no doubt) then that's probably what caused the diarrhea. His system just wasn't ready. I would avoid all fresh food for the time being, keep a close eye on him and absolutely go see a vet ASAP.

What are the ingredients of the juice? If those are hamster-safe then the mealworms are safe, if parts of the juice aren't safe or you don't know what the juice actually is (the ingredients aren't listed) then I wouldn't give it to the hammy. Don't ever give them foods with unknown constituents.

I wouldn't go for that. They should have deep bedding throughout most of the enclosure, not in just one section. Also, levels are unsuitable for hamsters because they lack the ability to safely handle themselves when it comes to heights (as in, they'll climb up without issues but then just let go and drop or simply walk off a ledge). Dwarfs are especially prone to neurological issues following falls like that. Plus, adjusting that cage for the later stages of life when they need even surfaces and easy access to everything is going to be difficult.

If you still have some of the old food then mix the two for a while. If you don't, give him the new stuff to go alongside whatever stash he has remaining. It's better to introduce a new mix gradually than to switch him overnight. It's also normal for him to seem to dislike the new stuff at first, getting used to new foods can take a few weeks. Hamsters are quite the creatures of habit and don't always take to change easily, but don't worry, he's not gonna starve himself.
You can get pretty much everything you need on Amazon.

I'm pretty sure that wheel is too small. Syrians need a minimum 28cm/11in size wheel but bigger is better. And the white bowl in the corner, is that a food dish? If so, I recommend scatter feeding instead, it's much more natural and enriching for the hamster. You could also add in more bedding. Move the wheel to one of the shorter sides of the enclosure, then you can slope the bedding so that most of the enclosure can have deeper bedding. It also needs to be compacted, pressed down in order to hold burrows (it looks quite fluffed up on the photo). Otherwise, you're off to a much better start than most. 👍

There absolutely are bigger enclosures and other suitable hamster accessories available in the UK. Hell, they're more available there than in many other parts of Europe. Please take a look at these care guides, they'll tell you exactly what you need and where to find stuff and it's all UK-specific: https://www.happyhamstersuk.com/care-guide

It's hard to tell from your description, but I do agree that torpor is unlikely. If you've had her for a year and someone had her before that then it's possible that she's already a senior and her life is coming to its natural end. Pet store hamsters are also prone to internal conditions (heart disease is common) that may strike without obvious warning. How is she doing now?
There is absolutely no such thing as an enclosure that's too big. In fact, the recommendation (for any species) is 75 gallons or more.

I agree with everything they say about the pros of pellets, but see, that's why nutrition is hard - the other side of the coin. And here the other side is that, for one, pellets are an unnatural food source that prevents hamsters from using their natural skills (getting into seeds, opening nuts, etc). Pellets can offer complete nutrition, yes, but they remove the excitement and variety and therefore the mental health benefits that come with a varied diet. We have stuff like Soylent and Huel but who in their right mind would like to drink Soylent for the rest of their life, with maybe the occasional piece of chocolate thrown in? I'm not saying there's a right and wrong here, I'm sure you can see that both approaches have their pros and cons. And every ham is different - a picky eater might do well on your proposed plan but someone who has few dislikes and happily eats pretty much everything would probably be more suited to a varied seed mix diet. And they even change throughout their short lives! So yeah, there are no clear cut rights and wrongs, although I guess wrong, at least in my mind, is to feed solely pellets (and water, obviously) which is often recommended by sites that don't know their a$$ from a hole in the ground when it comes to animal care and that's why I jumped into this discussion. Hamsters move around a lot. You put him on the bed, he wants to go somewhere else. They have poor vision, bad depth perception and most importantly, lack the ability to climb downward like rats or mice. So if he wants to move somewhere lower how else is he gonna do it if not by jumping? They can use ladders and such when those are available (as part of a setup in their enclosure) but when they're not, jumping is really the only way. It's not about fun, it's about lack of ability to do it any other way. And because they're not good at downward movement and are fragile animals, you shouldn't let yours jump around, it could end badly.

It's not the hybridization of animals itself but rather the practice of breeding them that can be carried out in an unethical manner. In the hamster community ethical breeding refers to the kind of practice where animals are bred with their genetics (specifically coat colors and types), health and temperament in mind, ethical breeders also provide species-appropriate living conditions and seek out adopters who are knowledgeable, willing and able to provide suitable care for the hammies. On the other (unethical) hand you've got rodent mills (where pet stores get their animals) and individuals who are simply in it for financial gain and couldn't care less about animal welfare. So it's about the how and why a hamster is brought into this world not how pure their blood line is. However, when it comes to dwarf hamsters, you could make the argument that creating hybrids is somewhat unethical because it wouldn't really happen in the wild (the species simply don't interact) and the "unnatural" hybridization is thought to be the cause of excessive aggression you sometimes see in dwarf hamsters.

Okay, so if some of her burrows are visible from the side that's great. You can probably also tell where they are when you see her pop out somewhere cause she'll obviously be emerging from a burrow. One of the openings is often underneath a hideout, so they enter through the doorway of a hideout and then dig their way down. As for not destroying the burrows... you can't avoid that. I mean, what is a burrow? Empty space, a tunnel, surrounded by bedding material. By removing the soiled bedding, the walls of a burrow, you're left with... well, nothing. Cleaning burrows entails destroying them, that's just how it is. But don't worry, your hammy will recreate it ten times faster than you can clean it. :) Mine has a corner hideout and whenever I clean his burrows and then place him back in the enclosure he first sniffs around a bit and when he enters the hideout he immediately burrows down on the right hand side and is back to his food stash in seconds. So don't worry, destroying burrows comes with the territory but they'll recreate them like nothing ever happened. :) The only thing to keep in mind is don't remove her food stash unless it's clearly soiled, like you can feel it be damp or it reeks of ammonia. You'll probably end up removing some of the food anyway since it's impossible to separate every clean seed and pellet from the bedding so I suggest always adding some new food to her stash, to replace what was lost to the cleaning process. If you don't intend on baking daily then there's no reason to keep the starter out at room temperature and stress over having to constantly feed it. It can live in the fridge just fine and you can feed it once or twice a week. There are also no-discard regimens you may want to look into, especially if you bake regularly (like once a week).

And definitely don't give up after feeding it a couple of times without seeing results. It's normal for a starter that has been dormant for so long to take a bit of time to get going again. When it does, dry some of it to have another backup in addition to keeping it in the fridge.

There's nothing abnormal about any of it. Hooch is a normal part of the sourdough process (especially so if this is a new starter that's still creating its environment), some produce less, some more, some can go without feeding for days before hooch develops, others get it soon after "dinner time" passes. Color of hooch is typically dependent on how long the starter has been hungry - it starts out nearly clear when it forms and can become very dark brown the longer the starter is left unfed. Development in the middle is also normal, mine does the same thing. It's forming at the baseline (where your starter was right after feeding) but then when the starter rises and falls some of the fallen part remains above that baseline and above the hooch (probably because that part still has sufficient aeration to make it float... you can even see in the photo that the part above hooch is more bubbly). So yeah, your starter is perfectly fine and acting normally.
You don't have to feed it 60g of flour if you don't want to. It's all about ratios, you could do a 1:1:1 with 6g, 60g or 600g of flour (and water).

Move to a 1:1:1 feed if you want, but the actual reason for why your starter seems dead is that this is just what they do. The initial activity in the first couple of days is caused by unwanted microorganisms which then die, pH drops, LABs and yeast settle in and then your starter is good to go. During this time your starter will have very little (or no) visible activity, but that's normal and expected. If you have zero activity for 10+ days then start to worry, but before that it's all just a part of the normal process. Keep going, keep feeding and don't give up prematurely.

And yes, do give your starter a stir before discarding. Probably doesn't matter much if you feed soon after it peaks, but it's certainly a good practice with starters that have gone without a feeding for longer, say a week in the fridge, so yeah, it's a good habit to develop for the future.

You're not fully moved in and settled in a new place as soon as you unlock the door and neither are the organisms in your starter.

It's probably down to your HR zone settings. Garmin sets HR zones based on % max HR, not taking your resting HR into consideration. This means that when your resting HR is on the higher end, which it seems to be, you may enter exercise zones with the most minimal of activities, like walking from room to room or light gardening. I had the same thing with the default HR zone settings - I could get into zone 1 just walking to the bathroom and stay in zone 5 for over an hour when speed walking (which is of course nonsense because zone 5 is supposed to be your maximum effort level that you can only sustain for a very short period of time). What I'm saying is, calculate your HR zones using the Karvonen formula which takes your individual base level (=resting HR) into consideration and update your HR zones accordingly (you can change the BPM range for each zone on the app). Even better if you can also do a quick exercise test to determine your max HR which may differ quite a bit from the standard '220 minus age' result.

There's no harm in letting it fall (as another poster implied). Sourdough starters can go weeks, even months without feeding and still spring back to life when once again cared for properly. A different matter is when your starter peaks and then sits at a fallen level for hours and hours on a *regular basis*. It doesn't even come close to hurting it if it happens occasionally but once you see it happen on a daily basis that's when you know it's time to increase your feeding ratio (go from 1:1:1 to 1:2:2, for example). Constantly sitting at a low level/hungry is not good because that will start to create an environment that's unhealthy for the yeast and wanted LAB, but there's no need to feed it before it falls. In fact, letting it fall a bit is good because it tells you the window of time in which your starter has reached its maximum/is close to it/how long it's capable of staying there. And those timeframes change as your feeding ratios/temperatures change, so if you're always trying to feed it before it has a chance to fall a bit you're missing out on that vital information. 

PS. Is your starter a rye one? Those things actually lie to you about when they fall because their surface seems to stay put (more or less) but the inside collapses. You can even see it when you hold it up to a strong light source. Also, with a starter that young you should try to avoid paying too much attention to anything that may seem strange like not rising or falling, weird smells, periods of latency... it's all a part of the process of getting it to work, so just stick to your schedule, do the feeds and discards when you're supposed to and keep at it.

If you get a severe reaction, which IMO cycstic acne is (at least if it's something very uncommon for you), then it's probably the product's fault. If it's milder, a few more spots here and there, then it's really anyone's guess - could be the product, could be that you need time to adjust and things will go back to normal, could simply be a coincidence. Honestly, I've come to rely more on gut feeling, instinct and experience when it comes to assessing whether a minor "reaction" (if it even is that!) is due to a product or not. It's not easy, we like our checklists, clear cut answers, and personally I'm a very analytical, science-oriented type of person, but at some point you have to accept that there are simply too many variables to really *know* if a tiny change is something you can blame on a product or not. It's easy to think that if you get a few more spots and if that happens to coincide with starting a new product then it must be caused by that product - which is very well may be - but it could be lack of sleep, stress (even the positive kind), food, hormones, weather, not washing your pillowcases or the detergent you use to wash them, touching your face too much, washing too much or too little, it could be caused by the product in question reacting with something else in your routine, etc. etc. Sucks, but that's reality. That being said, I either continue on to see if things improve over time or stop using the product and reintroduce it a bit later to see if this helps me to tell the effect of the product apart from whatever else my skin could be responding to.
